care: Augustine is frank that as a young man he lived in ways he later regretted, and that for many years he lived with a woman he did not marry, with whom he had a son. He describes his regrets without detail, and the lesson summarizes them briefly. The Confessions is a Christian book of prayer; the lesson presents Augustine’s beliefs as his own.

young.html: Augustine grew up in North Africa about 1,650 years ago, in a town that is now in Algeria. He was very clever, and he became a famous teacher of public speaking. His mother, Monica, was a Christian who prayed for him for years. Augustine himself searched for a long time, trying different ideas about God and the world, before he became a Christian too.

Later he wrote the story of his life as a long prayer to God. It is called the Confessions. In it he remembers small things too. Once, when he was sixteen, he and his friends stole pears from a neighbor’s tree. They weren’t even hungry; they threw most of them to pigs. Augustine spent pages asking himself: why did I do it? Just because it was forbidden?

young.name: gb-voyage
young.cap: Follow Augustine from his home town in Africa to Rome and Milan, and back. Tap Next stop.

young.html: In Milan he noticed something surprising: the bishop, Ambrose, read books silently, moving only his eyes. In those days most people read aloud, even alone, so Augustine wrote it down.

A memory walk. Augustine wrote that memory is like a huge palace with many rooms. Close your eyes and walk through your home in your mind. In each room, find one memory: a birthday, a game, a meal. Tell the memories to someone in the order of your walk. Did walking through the rooms help you remember?

full.html: Augustine was born in AD 354 in Thagaste, a small town in the Roman province of Africa. His mother Monica was a devout Christian; his father Patricius was not, until near the end of his life. Augustine studied at Carthage, taught rhetoric there, in Rome and then in Milan, where he heard Bishop Ambrose preach. He was baptized at Easter in AD 387, returned to Africa, and in AD 391 the people of Hippo Regius made him a priest. Soon afterward he became their bishop. He wrote the Confessions around AD 397–400, in his forties.
The book is written to God, from beginning to end. The Latin confessio means both confessing one’s faults and praising God. Augustine does both, and invites the reader to listen in.

full.text: Thou awakest us to delight in Thy praise; for Thou madest us for Thyself, and our heart is restless, until it repose in Thee.
full.author: Augustine
full.ed: A Library of Fathers of the Holy Catholic Church, John Henry Parker, Oxford

full.html: This sentence is the theme of the whole book: a restless search that finds its rest. Augustine tells his life not as a list of events but as the story of where his heart was looking for rest, and where, in his belief, it finally found it.

head: Books
What happens
rows: Infancy and school. He loved Latin stories, and wept for Dido in Virgil, but hated Greek and arithmetic drills.
Sixteen: the pear tree. Why do wrong for its own sake?
Carthage. Cicero’s Hortensius fires him with the love of wisdom. He joins the Manichees for nine years, then grows doubtful and moves to Rome.
Milan. Ambrose’s sermons; the books of the Platonists help him think of God as spiritual and of evil as a lack of good.
The garden in Milan, AD 386: “Take up and read.”
Baptism; his mother’s death at Ostia.
Memory, and who he is now, as he writes.
Time, eternity and the first chapter of Genesis.

full.html: By AD 386 Augustine believed Christianity was true, he says, but could not bring himself to change his life. Sitting in a garden in Milan with his friend Alypius, he wept.

full.text: So was I speaking, and weeping in the most bitter contrition of my heart, when, lo! I heard from a neighbouring house a voice, as of boy or girl, I know not, chanting, and oft repeating, “Take up and read; Take up and read.” Instantly, my countenance altered, I began to think most intently, whether children were wont in any kind of play to sing such words: nor could I remember ever to have heard the like. So checking the torrent of my tears, I arose; interpreting it to be no other than a command from God, to open the book, and read the first chapter I should find.
full.author: Augustine
full.ed: A Library of Fathers of the Holy Catholic Church, John Henry Parker, Oxford

full.html: He opened Paul’s letters and read a verse from Romans 13 urging the reader to leave behind a careless life and “put on the Lord Jesus Christ.” He writes that his doubts vanished. In Latin the children’s words are tolle, lege, now among the most famous words in Christian writing.
The later books turn from his life to great questions. Book XI asks what time is.

full.text: What then is time? If no one asks me, I know: if I wish to explain it to one that asketh, I know not: yet I say boldly, that I know, that if nothing passed away, time past were not; and if nothing were coming, a time to come were not; and if nothing were, time present were not.
full.author: Augustine
full.ed: A Library of Fathers of the Holy Catholic Church, John Henry Parker, Oxford

full.html: The past no longer exists and the future does not yet exist, so how can we measure a long or short time? Augustine’s answer is that we measure time in the mind: memory holds the past, attention the present, and expectation the future. He calls time a “stretching” of the mind (distentio animi). God, he holds, is not in time at all but in an eternal present.

Reading the Confessions as a modern memoir. Augustine leaves out most of what a biographer would want (his son’s mother is never named) and dwells on moments that show his inner search. And the last four books are not a life story at all, but reflections on memory, time and creation.

items: Autobiography: the Confessions is often called the first great autobiography in the West: a person looking with open eyes at his own inner life.
Philosophy: his questions about time and memory are still discussed by philosophers and psychologists.
Christian thought: for Christians of many traditions, it has been a classic of prayer and of the story of conversion for 1,600 years.

deep.html: Augustine grew up in a Roman Empire that had recently become Christian under Constantine, while many people, including much of the educated class, still followed the old religions. He moved between them: a pagan education in Virgil and Cicero, the Manichee sect, Platonist philosophy, and finally the Catholic Church of Ambrose. The Confessions records how he weighed each of these; it is his own account and judgment of them.

items: Why do people sometimes do wrong just because it is forbidden, like the pear theft?
What is time? Can you explain it to someone without using a clock?
Is your memory a part of who you are? If you forgot everything, would you still be you?
Can a person know what is right and still not be able to do it? What finally helps?

deep.html: Augustine’s next great work, the City of God, turned from one soul’s story to the story of all humanity. Petrarch, a thousand years later, carried a copy of the Confessions and said he opened it at random on a mountaintop, as Augustine had opened Paul. Rousseau, later on this ladder, wrote his own Confessions in the 18th century, but as a defense of himself before other people rather than a prayer.

questions: Augustine stole pears he did not even want. Have you ever done something just because it was not allowed? Why do you think people do that?
Monica prayed for her son for many years. What does it mean to keep caring about someone who is going the wrong way?
“If no one asks me, I know: if I wish to explain it, I know not.” What else is like that, easy to use but hard to explain?
Augustine noticed Ambrose reading silently. What small thing have you noticed about someone that surprised you?
Why might someone write their life story as a letter or prayer, rather than a report?
